item.title: Red Bull Paid $13 Million Over Its Wings Slogan
item.description:
Red Bull never gave anyone real wings, but in 2014 it agreed to a $13 million settlement over its famous "gives you wings" slogan. A customer, Benjamin Careathers, sued and argued the drink's performance and concentration claims were no better than the same caffeine in coffee.
Red Bull says its marketing was always truthful and did not admit any wrongdoing. It settled to avoid the cost and distraction of litigation. Buyers from 2002 to 2014 could claim $10 in cash or $15 in Red Bull products.

item.title: McDonald's Secretly Collects Rent From Its Own Owners
item.description:
McDonald's is not only a burger company. Executive Harry Sonneborn, who worked with Ray Kroc, pushed the idea of owning the land under restaurants and renting it to franchisees. The company set up a real estate arm to do it.
Today franchisees pay a royalty on sales plus rent on top, and rent is the bigger part. About a third of McDonald's revenue comes from rent.

item.title: The Pringles Can Designer Was Buried in One
item.description:
Fred Baur was the P&G chemist who designed the tall Pringles tube. When he died in 2008 at 89, he asked to be buried in a Pringles can, and his children honored the request. They bought an original flavor can hours before the burial and placed part of his ashes in it.
The rest of his ashes went in an urn buried beside it. Some ashes also went to a grandson.

item.title: Domino's Promised 30 Minutes. A Jury Ended It.
item.description:
Domino's built its fame on a bold promise: your pizza in thirty minutes or it's free. Then a St. Louis woman sued after a 1989 crash with a Domino's delivery car, saying the guarantee pushed drivers to rush.
In December 1993 a jury awarded her more than $78 million. Days later Domino's dropped the thirty-minute guarantee. The case was later settled for far less, and Domino's did not admit its drivers drove unsafely.

item.title: IKEA's Flat Pack Started With a Sawed-Off Table
item.description:
IKEA's famous flat pack has a surprising start. As the story goes, designer Gillis Lundgren could not fit a table in his car for a catalogue photo shoot, so he sawed the legs off. That moment made IKEA rethink how furniture is shipped.
The table went on sale as the Lövet with its legs in the box, and self-assembly caught on. IKEA brought the table back years later as the Lövbacken.

item.title: Nike Paid $35 for Its Swoosh Logo
item.description:
In 1971 Nike's founder Phil Knight hired Portland State design student Carolyn Davidson to design a logo. She invoiced $35. He said he didn't love it but it would grow on him. The Swoosh went on shoes that year, and in 1983 Nike thanked her with a gold Swoosh ring and Nike stock.
One cheap sketch became one of the best-known logos on earth.

item.title: Costco's $1.50 Hot Dog Hasn't Changed Price Since 1985
item.description:
Costco has sold its hot dog and soda combo for $1.50 since 1985. Its CEO has said the hot dog was losing money, and the answer to raising the price was no. So Costco built its own hot dog factories to cut the cost and kept the price.
Nearly 200 million combos were sold in fiscal 2023. The hot dog is a classic loss leader: the real product is the membership.

item.title: Taco John's Owned 'Taco Tuesday' Until Taco Bell Stepped In
item.description:
Taco John's, a small Wyoming chain, registered the phrase "Taco Tuesday" as a trademark in 1989, in every U.S. state except New Jersey. In May 2023, Taco Bell asked the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office to cancel it, saying nobody should own a common phrase.
Two months later, Taco John's gave up the trademark in 49 states. Its CEO said, "We're lovers, not fighters." The chain also donated $40,000 to charity.

item.title: Coca-Cola Gave Away Millions of Free Drinks on Purpose
item.description:
In 1887 almost nobody had tried Coke. So owner Asa Candler stopped selling it and started giving it away, with handwritten tickets good for one free glass.
The tickets spread through magazines and the mail. Roughly 8.5 million free drinks later, Coke was served in every state, and Coca-Cola is widely considered the first company to ever offer coupons.

item.title: McDonald's Monopoly Was Rigged by Its Own Security Chief
item.description:
McDonald's Monopoly game pieces could win a million dollars. But the man guarding them, an ex-cop named Jerome Jacobson, was secretly handing the winners to friends and family.
He worked in security at Simon Marketing, the company that ran the promotion. He passed winning pieces to recruits who posed as lucky winners and paid him a cut. The FBI investigated under the name Operation Final Answer, and dozens were charged in 2001.

item.title: Wrigley Mailed Free Gum to a Million Strangers
item.description:
Wrigley didn't start in gum. He started in soap — and gave away free baking powder to sell it.
When the baking powder outsold the soap, he switched to selling that. Then he gave away free gum with the baking powder — and the same thing happened again. In 1915, he mailed free gum, unsolicited, to about 1.5 million homes listed in US phone books, figuring anyone who could afford a phone could afford gum. He repeated it in 1919 to roughly 7 million homes.

item.title: Hoover Gave Away Free Flights. It Cost Them Millions.
item.description:
Hoover said: buy a vacuum, fly free.
In 1992, Hoover's British branch offered two free return flights to anyone who spent £100 on its products, and later added flights to the US. The cheapest qualifying vacuum cost about £120, but the tickets were worth far more. Hoover expected around 50,000 claims; hundreds of thousands came, and the bill reached tens of millions of pounds. Three top managers lost their jobs, and in 1995 Maytag sold Hoover's European business to Candy.

item.title: Pepsi's Ad Showed a Fighter Jet. He Sent $700,000.
item.description:
A Pepsi ad showed a fighter jet as a prize... so a student sent Pepsi a check for $700,000.
In 1996, Pepsi Points could get you T-shirts and leather jackets. The ad ended with a teenager landing a Harrier jet at school, for 7,000,000 Pepsi Points. A 21-year-old business student near Seattle saw that extra points cost 10 cents each, so the jet would cost about $700,000. A real Harrier was worth more than $20 million. He got investors to lend him the money and mailed Pepsi 15 points and a check for the rest.
Pepsi sent the check back and said the jet was only there to be funny. In 1999 a judge ruled no reasonable person could think the ad was a serious offer. And Pepsi's new ad? The jet cost 700,000,000 points.
⚠️ Dramatised: characters and scenes are illustrations. The facts are real. This is history, not investment advice.

item.title: Piggly Wiggly's Founder Tried to Beat Wall Street
item.description:
He invented self-service grocery shopping... then bet it all against Wall Street.
In 1916, Clarence Saunders opened the first Piggly Wiggly in Memphis. Instead of a clerk fetching your groceries, you walked through a turnstile, grabbed a basket and picked your own food, with a price on every item. He patented the idea, and by 1922 there were more than 1,200 stores.
When Wall Street traders bet his stock would fall, Saunders borrowed about $10 million and bought up most of the shares. One morning the price shot from $75 to $124 by noon. Then the New York Stock Exchange stopped trading and gave the traders extra time to deliver. The price fell, and Saunders lost his company and went bankrupt. But every time you pick your own groceries, you shop his way.

item.title: This Man Bought $3,000 of Pudding for Free Flights
item.description:
He bought 12,150 pudding cups... to fly for free.
In 1999, a California civil engineer named David Phillips noticed that a Healthy Choice promotion gave airline miles for product barcodes, and the cheapest item was pudding at about 25 cents a cup. He spent just over $3,000, had Salvation Army volunteers peel the labels in exchange for the pudding, and walked away with more than 1.2 million miles, lifetime Gold status with American Airlines and a tax write-off of about $800. His story even inspired part of a Hollywood movie.

item.title: Disney Secretly Bought a Swamp Using Fake Names
item.description:
Disney bought a secret swamp using fake names. One fake company was called "M.T. Lott"... say it fast.
Walt Disney wanted a huge new park in Florida, but if sellers heard his name, prices would explode. So his team bought swamp, scrub and cattle land through companies like Reedy Creek Ranch Corporation, for under $200 an acre. They gathered more than 27,000 acres, about twice the size of Manhattan, before a reporter cracked the secret in 1965.
